b: SALT LAKE CITY — The most interesting dinner in Salt Lake City might not involve a steak. In Albuquerque, it might not involve enchiladas. And in Cincinnati, it might have absolutely nothing to do with Midwestern comfort food.

Consider the options for exhibitors entertaining customers in Cincinnati: Eastern European cuisine at Sudova in the Central Business District, Vietnamese flavors at Pho Lang Thang near Findlay Market or British-Indian fusion at Marigold in the Convention District.
Venture farther and the menu opens onto West African, Uzbek, Central Asian, Nigerian, Peruvian, Nepali and Salvadoran cuisines.
Michael Sauer, CMP, Director of Convention Services at Visit Cincy
“The diversity of our restaurant scene gives us so many more ways to create memorable experiences for clients,” Michael Sauer, CMP, Director of Convention Services at Visit Cincy, said.

Cincinnati is part of a bigger American story. Immigration over the past decade has brought new communities — and new culinary traditions — to smaller and midsize cities that rarely featured in discussions of international dining.

An Associated Press (AP) investigation of federal records that covered about 4.5 million migrants entering the U.S. between October 2018 and July 2025 traced intended destinations well beyond New York City, Miami and Los Angeles, including Salt Lake City, Albuquerque and Cincinnati.

The records aren’t a census of where people ultimately settled, and not every restaurant can be traced to the recent arrivals. But newcomers are helping broaden the dining ecosystems available to convention groups.
For exhibitors, that means a new way to entertain customers: not just another reservation, but an introduction to a side of the host city guests never expected to find.
Cincinnati is a vivid example. According to the AP, migrants who named the region as a destination came from roughly 75 countries.

About 2,000 Mauritanians arrived in the small suburb of Lockland in 2023, joining an established West African community. Restaurants such as Touba Tedoungal reflect that cultural presence, although their suitability for large private events needs to be confirmed.
The international dining map extends beyond Lockland. A Fairfield initiative has spotlighted nearly 30 international restaurants.

Teranga Restaurant offers catering, while chef Gabi Odebode’s Afromeals develops African and Caribbean cooking classes, tastings and corporate events. That creates possibilities ranging from a small customer dinner to a chef-led gathering that feels less like a banquet and more like a shared discovery.

And exhibitors needn’t travel far. Sauer points to James Beard Award-nominated chef José Salazar’s recently reopened namesake restaurant, a block from the renovated First Financial Center, with expanded space and three private dining rooms.
Across the street, the Colombian-born chef also operates Mita’s, named for his grandmother and specializing in Spanish and Latin American cuisine.
James Beard Award-nominated chef José Salazar’s recently reopened namesake restaurant is a block from the renovated First Financial Center.

“When an exhibitor is entertaining customers in Cincinnati, the dinner is often just as important as what happens on the trade show floor,” Sauer says. “It’s an opportunity to build relationships, have meaningful conversations and give their clients an experience they won’t get anywhere else.”
His team’s role includes steering visiting groups toward unfamiliar restaurants and neighborhoods such as Over-the-Rhine, Walnut Hills and Northern Kentucky.
“Sometimes that means introducing them to a restaurant they’ve never heard of,” Sauer said.

The appeal isn’t that international food has suddenly arrived in Cincinnati. Many of these communities and restaurants predate the latest migration surge. It’s that a deeper, more visible mix gives organizers more ways to build the kind of hospitality that sticks in a customer’s memory.
The opportunity comes with a logistical catch: The independent restaurant everyone wants to discover may seat only 30 or 40 people. A trade show exhibitor may have 100 guests.

Tracy Stuckrath, Founder and Host of the Eating at a Meeting podcast and Founder, Speaker, Culinary Concierge and Consultant at thrive! meetings & events, advises starting with the kitchen, not the dining room.
“Ask how many covers the kitchen can turn out at once, not just how many seats there are,” Stuckrath said.
A 40-seat restaurant with a small crew may not be equipped to deliver dozens of multicourse meals simultaneously. Agree on a limited menu, service timing, staffing and payment before the event.

Stuckrath offers a model with decades of history: The Exhibitor Show’s (now EXHIBITORLIVE) “Dinner with Strangers” program, which organized tables of 10 at different local restaurants and let attendees sign up.

Diners paid their own tabs and shared the experience with fellow attendees. The system later moved online, but its central insight endures: You don’t have to put everyone in the same dining room to create a shared event.

For larger groups, Stuckrath suggests mixing small seatings with a chef-led welcome. She also stresses checking written allergen information, preventing cross-contact and arranging vegan, vegetarian, gluten-free and other dietary accommodations in advance. Accessibility and transportation require the same attention.

A compelling culinary story doesn’t replace reliable service. Nor should restaurateurs be treated as scenery: The best partnerships bring local owners and chefs into the experience as paid collaborators.
The old dine-around showcased the destination attendees expected to find. The new one introduces them to a city they never imagined.
